source.title: Can open source large language models be used for tumor documentation in Germany?—An evaluation on urological doctors’ notes
source.authors: Stefan Lenz; A. Ustjanzew; Marco Jeray; Meike Ressing; T. Panholzer

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including results, appendices, and declarations; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: It compares downstream task performance across pretrained language models of different parameter counts, but measures clinical-task performance rather than held-out pretraining loss or fitted scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream task performance, so it bears on V6. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or find compute-optimal allocations. Detailed prompt-variant results are in Figures 2–5 and Tables A-1–A-3; cited scaling-law results are not this study’s own results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates 11 off-the-shelf open models from 1.2B to 70.6B parameters on three German clinical extraction tasks and explicitly discusses performance against model size. That is a new-setting result bearing on V6. It is cross-sectional, not a controlled scaling sweep: training data, instruction tuning and 8-bit quantization (larger models only) all vary. It measures no loss, fits no curves and does no extrapolation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that 7–12B models offer the best balance and that larger models did not consistently outperform them. Models under 7B, and LeoLM (least total training data), performed worst. Llama 3.2 3B was not far behind the 7–12B models. Training method and data matter, not size alone.
record.recipe_differences: Cross-sectional evaluation of available models on German clinical documentation tasks; no controlled training-size or loss-scaling runs, power-law fits, or extrapolation.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt variants and number/domain of examples affect performance; the text reports less prompt-variant impact for larger models in Step 1 and substantial prompting variation in Step 3. Model training-data amount and training approach also differ across the evaluated models.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models (at least 7B) vary less across prompt variants; small models' sensitivity even falls with more few-shot examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt robustness and few-shot benefit increase with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Extra domain or German training (BioMistral, SauerkrautLM) does not beat the base models; LeoLM, with less total data, underperforms at 7B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream performance depends on total training data and training method, not parameter count alone.

record.peer_reviewed: BioData Mining; accepted for publication after peer review; the supplied text says it is not the Version of Record.
record.problems: The evidence is based on 149 snippets from 25 patients and only urological doctors’ notes; absolute performance may not generalize. Models differ in training data and training approach, so size is not isolated. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the cited comparisons, and prompt choice affects results. The study evaluates task performance, not pretraining loss or fitted scaling curves.
record.rows_left_out: The full prompt-by-model metric grids in Figures 2–5 and Tables A-1–A-3 contain many separately reported results. They are not exhaustively transcribed here; rows retain the text’s explicit cross-model size comparisons and the stated 92% first-diagnosis-date result. In particular, individual prompt-specific values and additional Step 2/Step 3 table entries are omitted.

untested.parts: Relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss; whether a fitted scaling curve predicts task performance; controlled size variation with data held fixed (only the Llama 3.x series approximates this).
No other modalities or training regimes.

missing.what: Per-model best accuracies for Step 1 (e.g. 1B 0.41, 3B 0.94, 8B 0.98, Mixtral 0.94, 70B 0.88, EuroLLM 0.56)
Step 2 snippet-correct proportions per model (7B–70B cluster near 0.86–0.89; 1B/EuroLLM far lower)
Step 3 accuracies per model (NeMo 0.92; 70B max about 0.84; small models below the 0.69 heuristic)

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is weak for scaling. It comes from a cross-sectional comparison of heterogeneous instruction-tuned models, with only the 3 largest models 8-bit quantized. Data are 149 snippets from 25 patients, with no uncertainty reported. Prompts were hand-designed and the best prompt was selected per model. The Table A-1 parse was reconstructed by column order, so the cited values should be checked against the original.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute scaling is measured.
No predictions from small-run loss fits or evaluations on runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law tests in other modalities or training regimes.

Tests selected German clinical documentation tasks across available model sizes, not a broad set of downstream tasks; does not relate task performance to pretraining loss or test whether a scaling curve predicts performance.
Does not fit or compare scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits, or test whether their values depend on counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated tumor-diagnosis detection against annotated snippets; authors identify it as the overall best model for accuracy in Step 1.

conditions.value: different prompting variants; best accuracy for the model

rows.value: overall best model in terms of accuracy
rows.note: The paper does not state a numerical accuracy for this comparison in the text.
rows.check: State should describe the size trend, not this model alone. Llama 3.1 8B has the best Step 1 accuracy (0.98, Table A-1), above Llama 3.1 70B (best 0.88) and Mixtral (0.94). Size gives no gain above 8B. The numeric values are readable in Table A-1 but were left out.

rows.subject: Mixtral 8x7B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated tumor-diagnosis detection; authors state that the largest models were not the best in this scenario.
rows.value: not the best model in this scenario
rows.note: No numerical accuracy is given for this statement.
rows.check: Mixtral 8x7B best Step 1 accuracy is 0.94 vs 0.98 for Llama 3.1 8B (Table A-1); the larger model brings no gain. The value should be numeric.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 70B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated tumor-diagnosis detection; authors state that the largest models were not the best in this scenario.
rows.value: not the best model in this scenario
rows.note: No numerical accuracy is given for this statement.
rows.check: Same-family comparison with the same 15T training tokens: Llama 3.1 70B best Step 1 accuracy is 0.88 vs 0.98 for 8B (Table A-1). Confound: 70B was run with 8-bit quantization.

rows.subject: Mistral NeMo
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated tumor-diagnosis detection; authors report performance very similar to Llama 3.1 8B.
rows.note: The statement describes similar task performance, not a numerical size trend.
rows.check: Mistral NeMo 12B best Step 1 accuracy is 0.94, similar to the 8B models; no gain with size. Different family and data.

rows.subject: EuroLLM 1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated tumor-diagnosis detection; authors report clearly weaker performance than the larger models.
rows.value: clearly weaker than the other, larger models
rows.note: Qualitative comparison; no single accuracy value is stated in the text.
rows.check: EuroLLM 1.7B best Step 1 accuracy is 0.56, far below the 7B+ models (0.88–0.98). Different family and data, so size is not isolated.

rows.subject: Llama 3.2 1B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated tumor-diagnosis detection; authors report clearly weaker performance than the larger models.
rows.value: clearly weaker than the other, larger models
rows.note: Qualitative comparison; no single accuracy value is stated in the text.
rows.check: Llama 3.2 1B best Step 1 accuracy is 0.41 vs 0.94 for 3B and 0.98 for 8B (Table A-1). Performance rises with size at the small end of the Llama family.

rows.subject: Llama 3.2 3B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated tumor-diagnosis detection; authors report performance very close to Mistral 7B.
rows.note: The smaller model is described as close to a 7B model, rather than showing a simple monotonic relationship.
rows.check: Llama 3.2 3B (best 0.94) is close to Mistral 7B (best 0.93) and well above 1B (0.41). This fits an increasing, saturating trend, not a non-monotonic one.

rows.subject: models with at least 7 billion parameters (group comparison stated by the authors)
rows.operation_detail: Compared model performance on tumor-diagnosis detection across prompting variants.
rows.value: examples had little impact on sensitivity for models of at least 7 billion parameters
rows.note: This is an author-reported group pattern; it is a prompting result, not a fitted scale relationship.
rows.check: This is a prompting (few-shot) effect within models, not performance as a function of scale. It belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: models with at least 7 billion parameters (group comparison stated by the authors)
rows.operation_detail: Compared ICD-10 coding task performance across models.
rows.value: performance of most models with at least 7 billion parameters was very close, except LeoLM
rows.note: The authors also state that Mixtral 8x7B and Llama 3.1 70B showed no clear advantage over the 7B–12B models.
rows.check: Step 2 ICD-10 coding: the authors see no clear advantage for Mixtral or Llama 70B over the 7–12B models. Table A-2 values (about 0.86–0.89 for both) are not transcribed.

rows.subject: Mistral NeMo
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated identification of first diagnosis dates using the best outputs from preceding steps.
rows.note: The authors identify this as the best result for the task.
rows.check: A single best-model value (NeMo 12B, 0.92) carries no size comparison by itself. It is a selection value. Could be relinked if paired with 70B's best Step 3 value of about 0.73–0.84 from Table A-3.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated identification of first diagnosis dates; authors report performance similar to larger models.
rows.value: performance similar to the bigger models
rows.note: No numerical value for this comparison is stated in the text.
rows.check: Step 3: Llama 3.1 8B is similar to the larger Mixtral and Llama 70B; no scale gain above 8B.

rows.subject: models with at least 7 billion parameters (group comparison stated by the authors)
rows.operation_detail: Compared performance across prompting variants for tumor-diagnosis detection.
rows.value: less impact of prompting variants on performance than for smaller models
rows.note: Prompt dependence is a source of variation in measured downstream performance.
rows.check: Prompt-variant stability is a stability measure, not task performance. It belongs under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Small-to-mid range, about 1B to 7–8B (notably Llama 3.2 1B → 3B → Llama 3.1 8B)
relationships.reason: Step 1 best accuracy rises from 0.41 (1B) to 0.94 (3B) to 0.98 (8B). EuroLLM 1.7B (0.56) is also far below the 7B+ models (V6-5, V6-6, V6-7).
relationships.display_finding: Best first-step accuracy rises from 0.41 at 1B to 0.94 at 3B and 0.98 at 8B, while EuroLLM 1.7B scores 0.56, well below models of 7B and larger.

relationships.condition: Above about 8–12B (Mixtral 8x7B, Llama 3.1 70B, 8-bit quantized) on all three clinical tasks
relationships.reason: Llama 3.1 70B scores below its same-data 8B sibling on Step 1 (0.88 vs 0.98). Larger models show no gain on coding or dates (V6-1, V6-2, V6-3, V6-4, V6-9, V6-11). Quantization and mixed model families confound this.
relationships.display_finding: Llama 3.1 70B scored 0.88 versus its 8B sibling's 0.98 on Step 1, with no larger-model gains on coding or dates, although quantization and model-family differences confound the comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Evaluated clinical documentation tasks across the tested model sizes
reader_labels.reason: Small models were generally weaker, but results also include a 3B model close to a 7B model and several larger models similar to smaller ones; task performance does not follow a simple, consistently increasing pattern (V6-1–V6-12).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Largest evaluated models on tumor-diagnosis detection and ICD-10 coding
reader_labels.reason: The 46.7B and 70.6B models were not the best on detection, and the authors report no clear advantage for the largest models in coding over models in the 7B–12B range (V6-2, V6-3, V6-9).
